description: How a government is formed, and the powers of the Prime Minister, cabinet and ministers.
content_html:
Forming a Government

After a general election, the leader of the political party that wins a majority of seats in the House of Commons is invited by the monarch to form a cabinet government. If no single party wins an outright majority, parties may negotiate a coalition or a confidence-and-supply agreement. In 2010, the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats formed the UK’s first peacetime coalition government since the 1940s, sharing cabinet posts between them.

The key distinction to understand is between the executive, which governs, the legislature (Parliament), which makes laws, and the judiciary, which interprets them. In the UK these three branches are not fully separated — members of the executive usually sit in Parliament — but they are meant to hold each other in check.

Key Fact

Government is formed by the party leader who commands a majority in the House of Commons. If no majority exists, a coalition or confidence-and-supply agreement may be negotiated.

The Role of the Prime Minister

The Prime Minister (PM) is the most powerful individual in government. The role has grown by convention rather than statute — there is no single law that defines it. Key powers of the Prime Minister include: appointing and dismissing cabinet ministers; chairing cabinet meetings; setting the government’s overall strategy; representing the UK at international summits; recommending dissolution of Parliament (subject to the Fixed-Term Parliaments Act 2011, which was itself repealed by the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022, restoring prerogative powers); and making senior public appointments.

The PM operates from 10 Downing Street in Westminster. Every Wednesday during parliamentary sessions, the PM faces Prime Minister’s Questions (PMQs) in the House of Commons — a key mechanism of parliamentary scrutiny where the Leader of the Opposition and any MP may question the PM directly. This is an important democratic accountability check: the PM must defend government policy in public.

Supporters of strong PM powers argue that clear leadership is essential for effective government: a PM who can appoint loyal ministers and set a clear agenda delivers on the mandate voters gave the winning party. Without these powers, government could become gridlocked.

Critics argue the PM’s powers have expanded too far, making the role closer to a president than a first among equals. They point to patronage (the PM appoints ministers, peers and public appointees) and the concentration of communications in Downing Street. Some argue this weakens cabinet government and Parliament’s scrutiny role. The debate reflects a genuine tension in an uncodified constitution where conventions can shift over time.

The Cabinet

The cabinet is made up of around 20–23 senior ministers who each lead a government department. Examples of cabinet positions include the Chancellor of the Exchequer (responsible for economic policy and the budget), the Home Secretary (responsible for policing, immigration and national security), and the Foreign Secretary (responsible for international relations). Cabinet ministers are appointed by the PM and are collectively responsible for government decisions.

Collective cabinet responsibility is a central constitutional convention: once the cabinet reaches a decision, all ministers are expected to support it in public. A minister who cannot do so is expected to resign. This maintains the appearance of unified government and prevents public division. Ministers who resigned during Brexit negotiations in 2018 — citing disagreement with the agreed approach — illustrated how the convention operates in practice.

Key Fact

Collective cabinet responsibility means all ministers must publicly support cabinet decisions. A minister who cannot support a decision is expected to resign from the cabinet.

Ministers and Government Departments

Below the cabinet, government is organised into departments, ministries and agencies. Each department is led by a Secretary of State (a cabinet minister) and supported by junior ministers — Ministers of State and Parliamentary Under-Secretaries of State — who manage specific policy areas. For example, the Department of Health and Social Care has the Secretary of State at the top, supported by several junior ministers responsible for areas like mental health, social care or public health.

The civil service is the politically neutral workforce that supports ministers. Civil servants do not change when a new government takes office; their job is to provide impartial advice, manage departments and carry out policy decisions. The most senior civil servant in a department is the Permanent Secretary. The separation between elected ministers (who set policy) and civil servants (who implement it) is an important constitutional safeguard.

Many students use “government” and “Parliament” as if they mean the same thing — but they do not. Parliament is the legislature: it is made up of all MPs in the House of Commons, all peers in the House of Lords, and the monarch in their constitutional role. Parliament’s job is to make laws and scrutinise the executive.

The government (the executive) is the party or coalition that holds power. It is made up of the PM, cabinet ministers, and junior ministers — typically around 100 people in total, out of a House of Commons with 650 MPs. So the government is a relatively small group that sits within the larger Parliament and is accountable to it. Parliament can remove the government through a vote of no confidence.

Accountability of Government

Government is held accountable through several mechanisms. In Parliament, MPs use questions, debates and select committees to scrutinise ministers. The National Audit Office checks how public money is spent. Courts can use judicial review to check that government decisions are lawful and do not exceed the powers granted by Parliament. Elections give citizens the ultimate power to remove a government that has lost public support. These overlapping checks reflect the UK’s commitment to the rule of law and parliamentary sovereignty.
exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Discuss question on the PM’s powers, avoid simply listing powers — examiners want you to weigh them. Present one viewpoint (e.g. PM powers are necessary for effective government) and then a contrasting one (e.g. PM powers have grown too great, undermining cabinet government). Use a real-world anchor: name a specific event such as PMQs, a resignation over collective responsibility, or the 2010 coalition negotiations. For a 12-mark Evaluate, your conclusion must add genuine evaluative thinking: decide which argument you find more convincing and explain why, citing a named example. Phrases like “it depends” without further criteria do not access the top band.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A government is formed when the party leader commanding a majority in the House of Commons is invited by the monarch to govern; if no majority exists, a coalition may be formed.
  • The Prime Minister chairs the cabinet, appoints ministers and sets overall strategy, while collective cabinet responsibility requires all ministers to publicly support cabinet decisions.
  • Government is distinct from Parliament: the government is the executive that governs; Parliament is the legislature that scrutinises, passes laws and can hold the government to account.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the role of the civil service?
A) To win elections and form a government
B) To provide politically neutral advice and implement government policy
C) To pass laws in the House of Commons
D) To appoint the Prime Minister
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for B) To provide politically neutral advice and implement government policy.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by collective cabinet responsibility.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks: 1 mark for stating that cabinet ministers must publicly support government decisions; 1 mark for adding that a minister who cannot support a decision is expected to resign.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the distinction between the executive and the legislature matters in a democracy.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying the executive as the government that runs the country; 1 mark for identifying the legislature (Parliament) as the body that makes laws and scrutinises the executive; 1 mark for explaining that the separation prevents any one body having unchecked power (e.g. Parliament can remove a government through a vote of no confidence); 1 mark for a developed consequence, such as that judicial review or PMQs provide additional checks, protecting citizens from unlawful government action.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

"A 2024 survey of 1,500 UK adults conducted by a civic research charity found that 62% of respondents could not name the role of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and 54% believed the Prime Minister was able to pass laws without a parliamentary vote. The charity concluded that low civic knowledge was a significant barrier to democratic accountability."

Using the extract and your own knowledge, what does this source suggest about the challenge of holding government to account?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying the key finding (majority cannot name the Chancellor's role or understand PM's legislative powers); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (if citizens do not understand how government works, they cannot effectively scrutinise it); 1 mark for using own knowledge to contextualise (e.g. Parliament holds the government to account through PMQs, debates and committees, but this only works if the public can follow and respond to these proceedings); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement (e.g. the source suggests civic education is essential to make democratic accountability meaningful, though the survey represents a snapshot and may not reflect all citizens).

practice_questions.text:
A local council is debating whether schools in its area should include compulsory lessons on how government works, including the role of the PM and cabinet. A school governor argues that students who understand the structure of government are better able to participate as citizens.

Discuss whether compulsory civic education about how government is formed and operates is a good way to strengthen democracy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear two-sided discussion with at least one named real-world anchor per side (e.g. the Citizenship Studies GCSE, the 2010 coalition and collective responsibility, PMQs as an accountability mechanism). Contrasting viewpoints are connected using evaluative connectives (however, on the other hand). A substantiated judgement weighs which argument is stronger and why.

Secure: Two-sided discussion with at least one named example (e.g. how coalition government changed cabinet formation in 2010, or the role of PMQs). Generally accurate; at least one viewpoint developed with a reason.

Developing: Relevant points made but mainly one-sided, or two sides listed without development. Little or no named real-world example.

Emerging: Basic points about government or civic education. Descriptive rather than analytical; no named example or substantiated judgement.

practice_questions.text:
"The Prime Minister has too much power in the UK system of government."

Evaluate this statement. In your answer, consider arguments in support of the statement and arguments against it, and reach a substantiated overall conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: The PM appoints and dismisses all cabinet ministers, giving enormous control over who governs. Collective cabinet responsibility can silence dissent. The PM also controls the government’s legislative programme and has significant patronage powers (appointing peers and public officials). Critics argue this concentration of authority in one individual undermines the collegial spirit of cabinet government.

Arguments against: The PM is accountable to Parliament through PMQs every week, through select committees and through votes of no confidence — Parliament removed the government’s majority several times between 2017 and 2019. Courts can use judicial review to strike down unlawful government decisions. The cabinet itself can withdraw support, as seen when ministers resigned over policy disagreements. The electorate removes a government at elections.

Mastering: Balanced evaluation with named examples on both sides (e.g. PMQs, resignation of ministers over collective responsibility, judicial review). Substantiated overall conclusion that goes beyond “it depends” — for example, arguing that while PM powers are significant, the overlapping checks of Parliament, the judiciary and public opinion mean they are not unchecked.

Secure: Two-sided argument with at least one named example. Conclusion present but may not fully justify the weighing.

Developing: Relevant points but mainly one-sided or lacking named examples. Conclusion present but thin.

Emerging: Basic points, largely descriptive. No named example, no substantiated conclusion.

knowledge_checks.q: Who invites the leader of the majority party to form a government after a general election?
options: The Speaker of the House of Commons
A written test taken by PM candidates before taking office
A weekly session in the House of Commons where MPs can question the Prime Minister
A committee that approves the PM's cabinet appointments
A monthly press conference held by the PM at Downing Street

knowledge_checks.q: The convention that all cabinet ministers must publicly support government decisions is called _____ cabinet responsibility.
The _____ is the politically neutral professional workforce that supports ministers in running government departments.
Match each role to its description:
right: Head of government who chairs the cabinet and appoints ministers
Cabinet minister responsible for economic policy and the budget
Most senior civil servant in a government department

flashcard_questions.q: Who forms a government after a UK general election?
flashcard_questions.a: The leader of the party commanding a majority in the House of Commons.

flashcard_questions.q: Who does the Prime Minister appoint and dismiss?

flashcard_questions.a: All ministers must publicly support cabinet decisions or resign.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened in 2010 that illustrates coalition government formation?
flashcard_questions.a: Conservatives and Liberal Democrats formed a coalition after no party won a majority.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the civil service's key constitutional feature?
flashcard_questions.a: It is politically neutral and serves whichever government is in power.
Courts checking that government decisions are lawful and within Parliamentary powers.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Parliament scrutinise the PM directly each week?
flashcard_questions.a: Through Prime Minister's Questions (PMQs) in the House of Commons.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between the executive and the legislature?
flashcard_questions.a: Executive governs; legislature (Parliament) makes laws and scrutinises the executive.

flashcard_questions.q: How many members does a typical UK cabinet have?
What is the most senior civil servant in a government department called?
How can Parliament remove a government that has lost its majority?
flashcard_questions.a: Through a vote of no confidence.

flashcard_questions.q: The convention that a minister who disagrees with a cabinet decision must _____.

glossary_terms.definition: The group of senior ministers who lead government departments and set policy, chaired by the Prime Minister.
The branch of government responsible for running the country day to day and implementing laws, headed by the Prime Minister.
The head of the UK government, who chairs the cabinet, appoints ministers and is accountable to Parliament.
The constitutional convention that all cabinet ministers must publicly support and defend collective decisions made in cabinet.
The permanent, politically neutral professional workforce that supports government ministers in running departments and implementing policy.
The process by which courts can review government decisions to check they are lawful and within the powers granted by Parliament.
